source.title: Does Learning Require Memorization? A Short Tale about a Long Tail
source.venue: Proceedings of the 52nd Annual ACM SIGACT Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC)

confidence_rationale: This is the honest counterweight to the other three entries. Feldman proves that on long-tailed data distributions, memorising atypical / low-frequency training examples is NECESSARY for close-to-optimal generalisation error. That does not overturn MECH-472's premise (held-out evidence is still the right test of acquisition), but it sharply qualifies the naive reading that ANY in-context-vs-held-out gap is pathological: some apparent 'memorisation' is functional, and a competence can legitimately retain instance-specific content it needed to learn the tail. Confidence is moderate because it is a theoretical result under distributional assumptions, and its bearing on MECH-472 is about calibrating the THRESHOLD, not the existence of the test.
failure_signatures: Because memorisation of rare examples is provably necessary for optimal generalisation on long-tailed data, a nonzero in-context-vs-held-out gap does NOT by itself imply the competence failed to generalise -- MECH-472's threshold must tolerate the functional memorisation the tail requires.

A promotion rule that treats any held-out gap as memorisation-and-therefore-block would suppress competences that legitimately encode tail-specific structure, harming generalisation rather than protecting it.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Under a mixture-of-subpopulations model of natural (long-tailed) data, algorithms that achieve close-to-optimal generalisation error must memorise labels of atypical, low-frequency training examples; memorisation is not merely a side-effect of over-parameterisation but a requirement for optimal learning when frequencies are long-tailed.
mapping.ree_translation: MECH-472 treats the in-context-vs-held-out gap as a memorisation-vs-acquisition signal to threshold. Feldman shows that not all instance-specific retention is bad: on realistic long-tailed task distributions some memorisation is exactly what an optimal learner must do. So the mapping to MECH-472 is that the gap is a graded, threshold-calibrated signal -- not a binary 'gap => memorised => reject'.
mapping.mapping_caveat: This is a theoretical result under a specific generative model (subpopulation mixture, long-tailed frequencies) about supervised classification error; it does not measure an agent's held-out competence directly, and 'memorisation' in Feldman's sense (retaining rare-example labels) is not identical to MECH-472's 'memorisation' (a competence that only works in its generating contexts). It bounds the STRONG interpretation of MECH-472, it does not test the claim itself.
mapping.source_context: Theoretical learning theory; supervised classification under a mixture-of-subpopulations data model; no agent, no RL, no biological data.

confidence_components.notes: High-quality theory (STOC) but its role is to calibrate MECH-472's threshold and guard against an over-strong reading, not to confirm or refute the core claim. The two senses of 'memorisation' are related but not identical, which is the main fidelity discount.
